standard_prerequisites.name: Irreducible components and generic points: an irreducible closed subset has a unique generic point, and the closure of the image of an irreducible subset under a continuous map is irreducible
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used at proof lines 1395-1396 to pass from the components Z_i of X to the irreducible subsets closure of f(xi_i) in S
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the generic points xi_i and the irreducibility of each f(Z_i).

standard_prerequisites.name: A morphism is dominant exactly when the closure of its image is the whole target, and the closure of a finite union is the union of the closures
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used at proof lines 1397-1399 in the display S = closure of f(X) = union of closures of f(Z_i)
standard_prerequisites.use: Turns the hypothesis that f is dominant into a finite union decomposition of S by irreducible subsets.

core_obligations: Assume f is dominant and write X = Z_1 union ... union Z_n for the decomposition of X into its finitely many irreducible components, with generic points xi_i satisfying Z_i = closure of {xi_i} (proof lines 1393-1395).

Use that each f(Z_i) is an irreducible subset of S and that taking closures commutes with finite unions to write S as the finite union of the irreducible subsets closure of {f(xi_i)} (proof lines 1396-1402).
Read off the two conclusions: every irreducible component of S has its generic point in the image of f, and S itself has only finitely many irreducible components (proof lines 1402-1404).
proof_roadmap: Decompose X into finitely many irreducible components with generic points xi_i (proof lines 1394-1395).
Push the decomposition forward along f and identify S with the finite union of the closures of the images of the generic points, then read off both conclusions (proof lines 1396-1404).
difficulty_reason: The lemma says that when X has finitely many irreducible components, dominance of f : X to S is equivalent to every irreducible component of S having its generic point in the image of f, and that S then has finitely many irreducible components as well (statement lines 1382-1390). The proof is a short but genuine topological argument: it decomposes X into components Z_i with generic points xi_i, uses that the image of an irreducible set is irreducible and that closure commutes with finite unions to obtain the display S = union of the closures of {f(xi_i)}, and then reads both conclusions off that display (proof lines 1392-1404). It is H2: the input is the generic-point dictionary for irreducible components, but the union-of-closures manipulation and the passage from generic points in the image to the statement about components are carried out inside the counted span.
